sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.quote: Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. ... Encourage your child to give their dummy away to the dummy fairy, or to another parent of a younger child. Give plenty of encouragement and keep it positive. Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Prepare the child a couple of days ahead, a chosen cuddly toy in the dummy's place, giving the dummy to the dummy fairy or a younger child, encouragement, and that the first few days are the hardest. An Australian state health service page, applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: When Should Kids Stop Using Pacifiers?
sources.publisher: Cleveland Clinic (pediatrician Jason Sherman, DO), 1 Jan 2026
sources.quote: “We typically recommend a gradual approach rather than making children quit cold turkey,” Dr. Sherman says. ... “Snuggling up with those special items offers them security and comfort throughout the night,” Dr. Sherman explains. ... “You may have to deal with a few days and nights of fussing,” Dr. Sherman concedes. “But stand firm.”
sources.supports: A gradual approach, a light blanket or stuffed animal for comfort through the night, and a few days and nights of fussing at the start. A US hospital health library page, used as general advice.

sources.title: Stopping use of a dummy and/or bottle
sources.publisher: Derbyshire Family Health Service (Derbyshire Community Health Services NHS Foundation Trust, no date shown)
sources.quote: Give your child plenty of comfort and distractions as you remove the dummy. Help them learn new ways to soothe themselves, such as using a favourite blanket or toy instead of the dummy. ... Try sending the dummy away to Santa, the Easter Bunny, the Tooth Fairy or the Dummy Fairy. ... all parents and carers (including childcare settings) should follow the same steps so the message is consistent and the child is not confused.
sources.supports: Plenty of comfort and distraction, a favourite blanket or toy instead, sending the dummy away to a fairy, and the same steps from every carer. NHS trust webpage for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Pacifier Weaning: When Is It the Right Time?
sources.publisher: Healthline (written by Rhona Lewis, medically reviewed by Karen Gill, M.D., 28 Aug 2020)
sources.quote: Explain to your toddler that in 3 days’ time, you’ll be taking away their paci because they’re already big enough to manage without one. ... Brace yourself against the tantrums and the crying, show the empathy that you surely feel (no one said it would be easy), but do not give in.
sources.supports: Tell the child a few days ahead, show empathy through the crying but do not give the pacifier back. A medically reviewed consumer page, not a clinical guideline.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library (no date shown)
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. Try to swap it out for their favourite toy or teddy to hold onto for comfort instead. ... Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child’s sight.
sources.supports: Limit the dummy to naps and bedtime, swap it for a favourite toy or teddy, and keep it out of the child's sight. NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (page dated 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with big feelings. The page is about empathy, not about the topic itself; used only as support for reading stories about a hard moment, with no promise of a result.

פעם הוא היה איתי בכל מקום 🌙
בסלון, באוטו, מתחת לשמיכה.
כשהייתי עייף, הוא היה בפה.
ובלילה, הוא היה הכי איתי.
אני בכלל לא שמתי לב.

ונרדמתי בלי לחשוב
מוצץ, כרית, ואור קטן בפינה.
העיניים נסגרו, והנשימה נהייתה איטית.
אמא ואבא, לא הייתי צריך
לחפש שום דבר.

ואז אמרתם לי מראש
ישבתם לידי על המיטה ואמרתם:
״עוז, עוד שלושה לילות, ואז לפיה.״
לא הבנתי הכל, אבל ידעתי
שמשהו משתנה.

דובי חום על הכרית
בחרתי אותו בעצמי, בחנות.
הוא מחכה לי כל ערב.
מה יעזור לי:
שתזכירו לי אותו, כשאני מבקש מוצץ.

בלילה אני עדיין קם
אני פותח עיניים בחושך,
והיד שלי מחפשת מוצץ.
אין. הלב שלי דופק קצת,
ואני קורא לכם.

ואז אתם באים, ואומרים
מה יעזור לי לשמוע:
״אנחנו פה, עוז. קשה בלי המוצץ.״
אתם לא מחזירים לי אותו.
אבל אתם לידי, וזה עוזר.

״ישנת בלי מוצץ!״
בבוקר אתם אומרים את זה שמח,
ואני מרגיש גדול.
מה יעזור לי:
פרגון, גם כשהלילה היה קשה.

דובי, כרית, ואתם לידי
אותו סדר כל ערב.
אני מחבק את הדובי,
ואתם יושבים לידי עוד רגע.
ואני נרדם כמעט כמו פעם.

sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.quote: Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. ... Encourage your child to give their dummy away to the dummy fairy, or to another parent of a younger child. Give plenty of encouragement and keep it positive. Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Prepare the child a couple of days ahead, a chosen cuddly toy in the dummy's place, giving the dummy to the dummy fairy or a younger child, encouragement, and that the first few days are the hardest. An Australian state health service page, applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: When Should Kids Stop Using Pacifiers?
sources.publisher: Cleveland Clinic (pediatrician Jason Sherman, DO), 1 Jan 2026
sources.quote: “We typically recommend a gradual approach rather than making children quit cold turkey,” Dr. Sherman says. ... “Snuggling up with those special items offers them security and comfort throughout the night,” Dr. Sherman explains. ... “You may have to deal with a few days and nights of fussing,” Dr. Sherman concedes. “But stand firm.”
sources.supports: A gradual approach, a light blanket or stuffed animal for comfort through the night, and a few days and nights of fussing at the start. A US hospital health library page, used as general advice.

sources.title: Stopping use of a dummy and/or bottle
sources.publisher: Derbyshire Family Health Service (Derbyshire Community Health Services NHS Foundation Trust, no date shown)
sources.quote: Give your child plenty of comfort and distractions as you remove the dummy. Help them learn new ways to soothe themselves, such as using a favourite blanket or toy instead of the dummy. ... Try sending the dummy away to Santa, the Easter Bunny, the Tooth Fairy or the Dummy Fairy. ... all parents and carers (including childcare settings) should follow the same steps so the message is consistent and the child is not confused.
sources.supports: Plenty of comfort and distraction, a favourite blanket or toy instead, sending the dummy away to a fairy, and the same steps from every carer. NHS trust webpage for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Pacifier Weaning: When Is It the Right Time?
sources.publisher: Healthline (written by Rhona Lewis, medically reviewed by Karen Gill, M.D., 28 Aug 2020)
sources.quote: Explain to your toddler that in 3 days’ time, you’ll be taking away their paci because they’re already big enough to manage without one. ... Brace yourself against the tantrums and the crying, show the empathy that you surely feel (no one said it would be easy), but do not give in.
sources.supports: Tell the child a few days ahead, show empathy through the crying but do not give the pacifier back. A medically reviewed consumer page, not a clinical guideline.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library (no date shown)
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. Try to swap it out for their favourite toy or teddy to hold onto for comfort instead. ... Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child’s sight.
sources.supports: Limit the dummy to naps and bedtime, swap it for a favourite toy or teddy, and keep it out of the child's sight. NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (page dated 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with big feelings. The page is about empathy, not about the topic itself; used only as support for reading stories about a hard moment, with no promise of a result.

sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health
sources.quote: Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. ... Talk about stopping the dummy for a couple of days to prepare your child. Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. ... Encourage your child to give their dummy away to the dummy fairy, or to another parent of a younger child. Give plenty of encouragement and keep it positive. Persist gently but firmly. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Prepare the child a couple of days ahead, a chosen cuddly toy in the dummy's place, giving the dummy to the dummy fairy or a younger child, encouragement, and that the first few days are the hardest. An Australian state health service page, applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: When Should Kids Stop Using Pacifiers?
sources.publisher: Cleveland Clinic (pediatrician Jason Sherman, DO), 1 Jan 2026
sources.quote: “We typically recommend a gradual approach rather than making children quit cold turkey,” Dr. Sherman says. ... “Snuggling up with those special items offers them security and comfort throughout the night,” Dr. Sherman explains. ... “You may have to deal with a few days and nights of fussing,” Dr. Sherman concedes. “But stand firm.”
sources.supports: A gradual approach, a light blanket or stuffed animal for comfort through the night, and a few days and nights of fussing at the start. A US hospital health library page, used as general advice.

sources.title: Stopping use of a dummy and/or bottle
sources.publisher: Derbyshire Family Health Service (Derbyshire Community Health Services NHS Foundation Trust, no date shown)
sources.quote: Give your child plenty of comfort and distractions as you remove the dummy. Help them learn new ways to soothe themselves, such as using a favourite blanket or toy instead of the dummy. ... Try sending the dummy away to Santa, the Easter Bunny, the Tooth Fairy or the Dummy Fairy. ... all parents and carers (including childcare settings) should follow the same steps so the message is consistent and the child is not confused.
sources.supports: Plenty of comfort and distraction, a favourite blanket or toy instead, sending the dummy away to a fairy, and the same steps from every carer. NHS trust webpage for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Pacifier Weaning: When Is It the Right Time?
sources.publisher: Healthline (written by Rhona Lewis, medically reviewed by Karen Gill, M.D., 28 Aug 2020)
sources.quote: Explain to your toddler that in 3 days’ time, you’ll be taking away their paci because they’re already big enough to manage without one. ... Brace yourself against the tantrums and the crying, show the empathy that you surely feel (no one said it would be easy), but do not give in.
sources.supports: Tell the child a few days ahead, show empathy through the crying but do not give the pacifier back. A medically reviewed consumer page, not a clinical guideline.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library (no date shown)
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. Try to swap it out for their favourite toy or teddy to hold onto for comfort instead. ... Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child’s sight.
sources.supports: Limit the dummy to naps and bedtime, swap it for a favourite toy or teddy, and keep it out of the child's sight. NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Helping Kids Learn to Take Turns and Practice Waiting
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Samantha Gratton), 4 Aug 2023
sources.quote: Learning how to wait takes practice. ... Waiting is hard (even for grown-ups)! ... Talking about what comes next can comfort your child and remind them who gets the next turn. ... (You can also use a timer that shows a countdown for taking turns!) ... Working through big feelings with your kids helps them feel seen and understood while they wait.
sources.supports: Waiting takes practice and is hard even for adults, so name the feeling, talk about what comes next, and give the child something they can see, like a countdown. A PBS KIDS parenting article written about turns and sharing, applied to waiting for a birthday.

sources.title: How to help your preschooler manage overexcitement
sources.publisher: Understood (written by Amanda Morin, expert review by Mark J. Griffin, PhD), 5 Aug 2019
sources.quote: Set up a signal that you both agree would work well to help your child know when it’s time to stop. Plan on giving a five-minute notice when you see they start to get louder and too excited.
sources.supports: A signal the parent and child agree on, and a notice before it is time to stop, help a preschooler who gets too excited. A parenting information page, used as general advice, not a clinical claim.

sources.title: Create a Kid’s Calendar in Two Ways
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents, 23 Jul 2018
sources.quote: Waiting for big events like birthdays, holidays, or the start of school are great opportunities to for your child to learn to keep track of days and months.
sources.supports: Waiting for a birthday is a chance for a child to learn to keep track of days, with a calendar the child helps to make. A PBS KIDS activity page.

sources.title: Is It Tomorrow Yet? Tips, Tricks, and Books for Helping Kids Learn How Calendars Work
sources.publisher: Brightly (Penguin Random House), by Lindsay Barrett
sources.quote: “How many more days until my birthday?” ... explanations like “on Wednesday,” “in a week,” or “in the fall” feel arbitrary when you’re little. ... Ask them to point to “yesterday, today, and tomorrow,” find specific day numbers, or count the days or weeks until a significant event.
sources.supports: Young children keep asking how long until their birthday, a time like in a week feels arbitrary to them, and counting the days on a calendar together gives them something concrete. A reading site article by a kindergarten and preschool teacher, general advice.

sources.title: Helping Kids Learn to Take Turns and Practice Waiting
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents (Samantha Gratton), 4 Aug 2023
sources.quote: Learning how to wait takes practice. ... Waiting is hard (even for grown-ups)! ... Talking about what comes next can comfort your child and remind them who gets the next turn. ... (You can also use a timer that shows a countdown for taking turns!) ... Working through big feelings with your kids helps them feel seen and understood while they wait.
sources.supports: Waiting takes practice and is hard even for adults, so name the feeling, talk about what comes next, and give the child something they can see, like a countdown. A PBS KIDS parenting article written about turns and sharing, applied to waiting for a birthday.

sources.title: How to help your preschooler manage overexcitement
sources.publisher: Understood (written by Amanda Morin, expert review by Mark J. Griffin, PhD), 5 Aug 2019
sources.quote: Set up a signal that you both agree would work well to help your child know when it’s time to stop. Plan on giving a five-minute notice when you see they start to get louder and too excited.
sources.supports: A signal the parent and child agree on, and a notice before it is time to stop, help a preschooler who gets too excited. A parenting information page, used as general advice, not a clinical claim.

sources.title: Create a Kid’s Calendar in Two Ways
sources.publisher: PBS KIDS for Parents, 23 Jul 2018
sources.quote: Waiting for big events like birthdays, holidays, or the start of school are great opportunities to for your child to learn to keep track of days and months.
sources.supports: Waiting for a birthday is a chance for a child to learn to keep track of days, with a calendar the child helps to make. A PBS KIDS activity page.

sources.title: Is It Tomorrow Yet? Tips, Tricks, and Books for Helping Kids Learn How Calendars Work
sources.publisher: Brightly (Penguin Random House), by Lindsay Barrett
sources.quote: “How many more days until my birthday?” ... explanations like “on Wednesday,” “in a week,” or “in the fall” feel arbitrary when you’re little. ... Ask them to point to “yesterday, today, and tomorrow,” find specific day numbers, or count the days or weeks until a significant event.
sources.supports: Young children keep asking how long until their birthday, a time like in a week feels arbitrary to them, and counting the days on a calendar together gives them something concrete. A reading site article by a kindergarten and preschool teacher, general advice.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (page dated 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with big feelings. The page is about empathy, not about the topic itself; used only as support for reading stories about a hard moment, with no promise of a result.
